back: Find the $k$ training points closest to $x$ and predict their majority class (regression: their mean target).
Smoothing parameter: small $k$ is low bias/high variance, large $k$ is high bias/low variance; choose by validation.
As $N\to\infty$ the 1-NN error rate is at most twice the minimum achievable (Bayes) error.
Euclidean distance sums squared raw differences, so large-unit features dominate. Standardise with training statistics.
In high dimensions all points are nearly equally distant, neighbourhoods are no longer local, and $O(Nd)$ search per query is costly.
No training; stores all data; each prediction computes $N$ distances ($O(Nd)$) unless an index is used.
$p(C_k|x)\propto p(C_k)\,p(x|C_k)$; predict the class with the largest value.
Features are conditionally independent given the class: $p(x|C_k)=\prod_ip(x_i|C_k)$.

front: Naive Bayes prediction in log space
back: $\hat y=\arg\max_k\ \log p(C_k)+\sum_i\log p(x_i|C_k)$; for multinomial: `X @ log_theta.T + log_prior`.
$\theta_{ki}=(n_{ki}+\alpha)/(\sum_in_{ki}+\alpha V)$, $n_{ki}$ = count of word $i$ in class $k$.
An unseen word would give probability 0 and wipe out the whole product; the pseudo-count $\alpha$ keeps all probabilities positive (a Dirichlet prior).
Per class and feature: mean $\mu_{ki}$, variance $\sigma_{ki}^2$; $\log p(x_i|C_k)=-\frac12\log(2\pi\sigma^2)-\frac{(x_i-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}$.

front: Why naive Bayes still works / where it fails
back: Only the argmax matters and few parameters means low variance; fails when correlated features carry the label signal (e.g. XOR) and probabilities are over-confident.
